--- title: "Simulation Based Estimation of Sampling Bias" jupyter: python3 fig-dpi: 300 bibliography: references.bib --- ```{=html} ``` # Data and models **Field.** GLORYS12V1 reanalysis on its native $1/12^\circ$ grid. OHC is the $0$–$2000$ m depth integral of potential temperature against constant $c_p\rho$ (`code/ohc.py`), evaluated daily over 2010–2019. Cells enter the analysis only where $\mathrm{deptho} > 2000$ m *and* the integral is defined at every level, which is $92.4\%$ of Box B by area ($26{,}785$ cells) and $99.8\%$ of Box A ($34{,}863$ cells) — Box B loses its shelf edge, Box A is essentially all deep ocean. **Mean field.** OHC is split as $\mathrm{OHC} = \hat m + \tilde Z$ into a smooth climatological mean field $\hat m$, fitted once across $1995$–$2019$, and the residual $\tilde Z_k$ the designs actually sample — the field the sampling bias is defined over. $\hat m$ is a per-cell OLS on a quadratic trend plus annual and semiannual harmonics, fit against the GLORYS *monthly* record with each basis function averaged over its month to match the monthly-mean response, then evaluated pointwise per day. @sec-meanfield gives the estimator and summarizes what it leaves. **Advection.** OceanParcels, park depth $1000$ m, advected by GLORYS daily $(u,v)$ over $15$–$50^\circ$ N, $70$–$30^\circ$ W. Floats advect continuously at park depth and record a position every $10$ days; there is no ascent, descent or surface drift, so a cycle is a position sample, not a simulated dive. Floats are deleted on leaving the velocity domain and retired at a lifespan drawn from the real Argo record for this region ($153$ deployments, median $1339$ d). **Estimation.** $\hat Z$ is the unweighted mean of $\tilde Z_k$ at the profile positions, and $\bar Z_k$ is the exact $\mathbb{P}$-weighted domain mean of the same field. # The analysis domain Two analysis boxes sit inside the downloaded GLORYS region, both spanning $60^\circ$–$40^\circ$ W: **Box B** ($35$–$45^\circ$ N) straddles the North Atlantic Current and the Gulf Stream extension, and **Box A** ($22$–$34^\circ$ N) sits in the quiescent subtropical gyre. Temperature is downloaded over a common buffer, from which the OHC truth and the fitted mean field are built; velocity is downloaded over a larger region, because floats seeded near a box advect well outside it and return, and a float that leaves the velocity domain is lost from the experiment rather than merely lost from the box. ::: {#cell-fig-domain .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The two analysis boxes (filled) inside the downloaded GLORYS velocity and thetao regions (dashed).](osse_files/figure-html/fig-domain-output-1.png){#fig-domain width=821 height=716} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-bathy .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![GLORYS ocean depth over the advection domain (left) and the sub-2000 m cells excluded from the analysis (right), both boxes outlined.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-bathy-output-1.png){#fig-bathy width=1402 height=605} ::: ::: @fig-bathy is why the analysis mask is not the whole box. OHC is integrated to $2000$ m, so a cell enters the estimand only where the water column reaches that depth; $88.7\%$ of the ocean cells in the advection domain do. The cut is not evenly distributed. **Box B loses $7.2\%$ of its area to it**, and that loss is concentrated in one corner: $99\%$ of its excluded cells lie north of $42^\circ$ N and $81\%$ west of $50^\circ$ W, on the Grand Banks and the Newfoundland shelf and rise. **Box A loses $0.08\%$** — $29$ cells, all isolated ridge and seamount tops in its eastern half. Median depth is $4.85$ km in Box B and $4.94$ km in Box A. The mask actually used is slightly stricter than the depth cut alone: it also requires the depth integral to be defined at every level, which drops a further $0.5\%$ of Box B and $0.15\%$ of Box A. Retained area is $92.35\%$ and $99.77\%$ against $92.83\%$ and $99.92\%$ from depth alone. ::: {#cell-fig-days .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Residual field Z (GJ per m2) on days at the 5th, 50th and 95th percentile of the combined daily spatial dispersion, both boxes on one shared diverging scale.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-days-output-1.png){#fig-days width=1403 height=535} ::: ::: @fig-days is the field the designs actually sample, shown unaveraged: each column is one real day with both boxes drawn on the same map, selected by where the combined-domain spatial dispersion $\mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(\tilde Z_k(\cdot,\tau))$ falls in the distribution of all $3{,}650$ days. Both boxes share one colour scale, so the western-boundary and subtropical amplitudes contrast directly. The same construction applied to the flow that moves the floats gives @fig-vel-u and @fig-vel-v: the two park-depth velocity components, each on the day whose combined-domain $\mathbb{P}$-weighted spatial standard deviation sits at the 5th, 50th and 95th percentile of that component's $3{,}650$ daily values. The velocity archive is on the identical native grid and is defined at every cell of the analysis mask, so these are the same measure $\mathbb{P}$ and the same cells as @fig-days — no regridding and no second mask. Values are interpolated to the $1000$ m park depth between the two archived levels ($902$ and $1062$ m), which is what Parcels does to the same files when it advects the floats. ::: {#cell-fig-vel-u .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Eastward velocity at 1000 m (cm/s), both boxes on one shared diverging scale.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-vel-u-output-1.png){#fig-vel-u width=1403 height=535} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-vel-v .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Northward velocity at 1000 m (cm/s), both boxes on one shared diverging scale.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-vel-v-output-1.png){#fig-vel-v width=1403 height=535} ::: ::: **The flow is roughly twice as disperse in Box B, and that holds on every day, not just energetic ones.** Median daily $\mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}$ is $12.1$ cm/s eastward and $11.5$ northward in Box B against $5.5$ and $5.4$ in Box A, and the decade-wide range of that daily value is narrow in both — $9.7$–$14.8$ and $9.0$–$14.7$ in Box B, $4.5$–$7.0$ and $4.4$–$6.7$ in Box A. The 5th and 95th percentile columns are therefore much closer to each other than the two rows are, so the box, not the day, is what sets the scale. **Box B's structure is substantially standing, Box A's is substantially transient.** The $\mathbb{P}$-weighted spatial sd of the decade-mean velocity field is $4.11$ cm/s eastward and $2.37$ northward in Box B against $0.94$ and $0.61$ in Box A — a $4.4\times$ and $3.9\times$ gap, about twice the gap in the daily dispersion. As a fraction of each box's mean daily spatial sd, the persistent part is $0.34$ and $0.21$ in Box B against $0.17$ and $0.11$ in Box A. **Neither box has appreciable net transport.** The domain-mean velocity is within $\pm 1$ cm/s of zero on every one of the $3{,}650$ days in both components and both boxes (largest $0.996$ cm/s), so the contrast between the boxes is in spatial structure, not in bulk flow through the domain. Together with @fig-days this is the setup the two boxes were selected to contrast: they differ $3.3\times$ in field amplitude and $2.2\times$ in the daily spatial dispersion of the flow that samples it, with the standing component of that flow differing by about $4\times$. # Mean field {#sec-meanfield} The sampling-bias question concerns the *residual* OHC field, not the total. The smooth climatological part of OHC is large and slowly varying, and any array recovers it almost exactly, so the bias $B$ lives entirely in what remains once it is removed. We therefore decompose $$\mathrm{OHC}(c,t) \;=\; \hat m(c,t) \;+\; \tilde Z(c,t),$$ with $\hat m$ a mean field fitted once across all years — a climatology, deliberately not a per-year fit — and $\tilde Z_k$ the year-$k$ residual the designs sample. Because $\hat m$ is estimated, so is $\tilde Z$; this section states the estimator and summarizes what it leaves. **Regression.** For each analysis cell $c$, OHC is modelled as $\mathrm{OHC}(c,t) = \phi(t)^\top \beta_c + \varepsilon(c,t)$ on the trend-plus-harmonics basis $\phi(t) = \bigl(1,\,t,\,t^2,\,\sin 2\pi t,\,\cos 2\pi t,\,\sin 4\pi t,\,\cos 4\pi t\bigr)^\top$ ($t$ in years): a quadratic secular trend and the annual and semiannual cycles. The coefficients are fit by ordinary least squares to the $1995$–$2019$ GLORYS *monthly* record. **Fit and prediction use different bases, on purpose.** A GLORYS monthly file holds the month *mean* OHC over $I_m = [t_0^m, t_1^m)$ but is time-stamped at its start $t_0^m$. Regressing that mean on the instantaneous basis $\phi(t_0^m)$ would misdate the harmonics by $\sim\!15$ d and attenuate their amplitude, since the mean of a sinusoid over a month is not its value at a point. We instead regress on the **window-averaged basis** $\bar\phi(I_m) = |I_m|^{-1}\!\int_{I_m}\phi(t)\,dt$, so both sides of the regression are monthly averages; each column is exact in closed form (constant $\mapsto 1$; linear $\mapsto$ the window midpoint; quadratic $\mapsto (t_1^3 - t_0^3)/3|I_m|$; each harmonic $\mapsto$ its exact windowed integral). The window is common to every cell, so there is a single design matrix $\bar X = \bigl[\bar\phi(I_m)^\top\bigr]_m$ and the per-cell fit is one pseudo-inverse, $\hat\beta_c = \bar X^{+} Y_c$. **Prediction is then pointwise:** the fitted field is evaluated at each instant on the daily grid, $\hat m(c,t) = \phi(t)^\top \hat\beta_c$, and subtracted from daily OHC to give $\tilde Z_k = \mathrm{OHC}_k - \hat m$ on the same mask. The window average enters only the fit, to keep regressor and response on the same footing; the prediction is the smooth curve itself. ::: {#cell-fig-meanfield .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Fitted mean field (quadratic trend plus annual and semiannual harmonics) at mid-month 2015, both boxes on one shared scale, in GJ per m2.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-meanfield-output-1.png){#fig-meanfield width=1484 height=472} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-decomp3 .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The OHC = mean field + residual decomposition on one shared day, both boxes drawn per field, in GJ per m2.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-decomp3-output-1.png){#fig-decomp3 width=1469 height=681} ::: ::: In @fig-decomp3 the identity $\mathrm{OHC} = \hat m + \tilde Z$ holds exactly on the analysis mask: the OHC panel is reconstructed from the other two rather than re-integrated from temperature, and reproduces the GLORYS field bitwise. OHC runs $60$–$90$ GJ/m$^2$ and is almost entirely captured by the smooth mean field; $\tilde Z$ is a few GJ/m$^2$ of mesoscale structure. On the shared day shown ($2010$-$02$-$26$), Box B's domain-mean OHC is $66.7$ GJ/m$^2$ against a mean field of $66.4$ (a $+0.3$ residual) and Box A's $79.8$ against $80.2$ (a $-0.5$ residual). The mean field varies on two time scales, neither daily: the harmonics move the Box B domain mean by $3.80$ GJ/m$^2$ within a year ($1.50$ in Box A), the trend by $2.59$ across 2010–2019 ($0.96$), and consecutive days by $0.03$. Everything mesoscale and day-to-day is therefore left in $\tilde Z$ — the field whose domain mean the sampling must recover. ::: {#cell-fig-ohc-series .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Daily domain-mean OHC with the fitted mean field (top) and their difference, the domain-mean anomaly (bottom), per box over 2010-2019 in GJ per m2.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-ohc-series-output-1.png){#fig-ohc-series width=1199 height=704} ::: ::: @fig-ohc-series shows this directly: each box's total OHC oscillates seasonally about its smooth mean field, and the residual gap — the domain mean of $\tilde Z$ — is a few GJ/m$^2$, larger and more variable in Box B than in Box A. **Stationarity caveat.** A single global trend-plus-harmonics form is a preliminary, stationary-in-form choice; OHC is strongly non-stationary across these current regions, so a covariance-aware mean is a likely refinement. It does not threaten $B$: a spatially uniform misfit in $\tilde Z_k$ differences out of $B$ identically, and the per-year residual offsets it leaves are carried explicitly in the residual-field table rather than assumed zero. # Estimand, truth, and estimator Let $\mathbb{P}$ be the normalized area $\times$ time probability measure on the Box B analysis domain: the base measure is surface measure restricted to the wet native GLORYS cells ($\mathrm{deptho} > 2000$ m, intersected with the data support), $A_c = e1t_c\,e2t_c$, tensored with counting measure on the $365$ days of the year and normalized. The target is the residual field's domain mean, $$\bar Z_k \;=\; \int_{\mathcal{X}} \tilde Z_k \, d\mathbb{P},$$ for each analysis year $k$, where $\tilde Z_k$ is the year-$k$ OHC 0–2000 m field with the fitted mean field removed. A design is a finite point set $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{n} \subset \mathcal{X}$ — the year-$k$ in-box profiles of one deployment realization $d$; its estimator and bias are $$\hat Z^{(d)}_k \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde Z_k\!\left(x_i^{(d)}\right), \qquad B^{(d)}_k \;=\; \hat Z^{(d)}_k - \bar Z_k .$$ $\tilde Z_k$ is a simple function on the native $1/12^\circ \times$ daily grid, so evaluating it at $x_i$ is the cell-day lookup of the *containing* cell, not an interpolation — no quadrature remainder enters. ::: {#00b5bb25 .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

The dispersion $\mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(\tilde Z_k)$ — $6.3$–$7.6$ GJ/m$^2$ in Box B against $1.7$–$2.4$ in Box A, and rising through the decade in Box B — is the $\sigma_k$ that any cross-box comparison of $B$ must be standardized by. # Deployment One continuous advection per realization generates the sampling. For realization $d$, $N$ floats are seeded uniformly over normalized spacetime across the velocity record — area-uniform over the deep ($\mathrm{deptho} \ge 1000$ m) part of a single region spanning both boxes plus an $8^\circ$ margin, uniform in release time — and advected once at park depth. A profile is scored against whichever box contains it, so one deployment feeds both boxes. The lead from the deployment start to the first scored year (several years, against an empirical lifespan median of $1339$ d) brings the drifting array to renewal equilibrium, so the in-box standing stock is flat across the analysis years by construction, with no calibrated release schedule. Each realization therefore yields $B^{(d)}_k$ for every analysis year at once, flow and field the same calendar year — there is no velocity-year / field-year pairing, only the realized diagonal. **How a float is advected.** Each float is carried by GLORYS12V1 daily horizontal velocity $(u,v)$ at a fixed park depth of $1000$ m and held there for its whole life — there is *no dive cycle*. The two archived velocity levels bracketing $1000$ m ($902$ and $1062$ m) are linearly interpolated to the park depth (as OceanParcels does natively), and the float is stepped forward by fourth-order Runge–Kutta at a $1$-hour time step. Its position is written every $10$ days, and that recorded park-depth position is taken as the profile — the point where a real float would begin its ascent — so a cycle is a position sample, not a simulated dive. A float is deleted when it leaves the velocity domain and retired at a lifespan drawn from the real Argo record (median $1339$ d). Relative to a real Argo cycle this omits the ascent, the roughly one-day surface drift, and the descent; the recorded $1000$ m position therefore differs slightly from the true surface profile position, and how much that simplification matters is exactly what the real-deployment comparison below tests. ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Simulated advection ::: {#cell-fig-advection .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![One simulated deployment: 60 float drift tracks and their 10-day profile points coloured by year, only in-box profiles (filled) entering an estimate.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-advection-output-1.png){#fig-advection width=947 height=722} ::: ::: ### Real Argo ::: {#cell-fig-advection-argo .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Real Argo trajectories over the same domain and years (60 of 740 floats) coloured by year, on the same base map for comparison.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-advection-argo-output-1.png){#fig-advection-argo width=947 height=722} ::: ::: ::: The two maps share the base map, years, and colour scale. The simulated array is seeded uniformly in space–time; real Argo is deployed programmatically, so its coverage is patchier and grows through the decade, but individual drift paths trace the same circulation — the contrast is in *where and when floats are placed*, not in the advection itself. **Reference.** An $n$-matched iid draw from $\mathbb{P}$ (cell $\propto A_c$, day-of-year uniform) is a genuine sample from $\mathbb{P}$ with $\mathbb{E}[B] = 0$ — the null reference and an end-to-end check of the gather, the day-of-year indexing, and the $\bar Z_k$ subtraction. Because it needs no advection it is drawn as a large ensemble ($2{,}000$ per box-year, at the year's median $n$), so its mean is a precise zero rather than a noisy few-draw estimate; its $5$–$95\%$ spread is the scatter of one uniform array of the same size. # The sampling weight field The bias is a projection, $B^{(d)}_k = \langle \tilde Z_k,\, w^{(d)} - p\rangle$, the inner product of the residual field with the excess of the empirical sampling weight over the uniform weight $p_{c,\tau} = A_c / (\sum_c A_c \cdot 365)$. One realization's sampling is the normalized empirical measure $$w^{(d)} \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \delta_{x_i}$$ on the spacetime domain $\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{T}$ — the wet native cells $\mathcal{C}$ and the $365$ days $\mathcal{T}$ — and averaging it over realizations gives $\mathbb{E}[w]$, the normalized occupancy (intensity) measure of the advective array, with $\mathbb{E}[B_k] = \langle \tilde Z_k,\, \mathbb{E}[w] - p\rangle$. $\mathbb{E}[w]$ lives on spacetime; we show it through its **spatial marginal**, the pushforward of $w$ under the projection $\pi:(c,\tau)\mapsto c$, $$w^{\mathrm{sp}}_c \;=\; \sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}} w_{c,\tau} \;=\; \frac{\#\{\,i : x_i \in c\,\}}{n},$$ the fraction of a realization's profiles that fall in cell $c$, summed over all days. The maps below show $\mathbb{E}[w^{\mathrm{sp}}_c]$ — the expected such fraction, i.e. the array's normalized spatial intensity — over the scored years $2015$–$2019$ on the native $1/12^\circ$ grid, against the uniform area marginal $p^{\mathrm{sp}}_c = A_c / \sum_{c'} A_{c'}$, as the ratio $q_c = \mathbb{E}[w^{\mathrm{sp}}_c] / p^{\mathrm{sp}}_c$ ($=1$ under area-fair sampling). The temporal marginal is flat by construction — the fixed $10$-day cadence, uniform release phase, and equilibrium stock leave no seasonal preference — so it is not shown; note only that $B_k$ is the *joint* spacetime inner product and does not split additively into space and time, a space–time interaction remaining (the decomposition table). ## Spatial marginal ::: {#cell-fig-wspace .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Over- and under-sampling log2(E[w]/uniform) on the native 1/12 deg grid, both boxes on one map per scored year and one shared scale (red over-sampled, blue under, white uniform).](osse_files/figure-html/fig-wspace-output-1.png){#fig-wspace width=1677 height=417} ::: ::: The per-cell weight distribution about the uniform value of 1, one panel per year: ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Box B ::: {#cell-fig-whist .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Box B distribution of the per-cell weight E[w]/uniform over native cells per year, about the uniform value of 1 (red line).](osse_files/figure-html/fig-whist-output-1.png){#fig-whist width=1417 height=318} ::: ::: ### Box A ::: {#cell-fig-whist-a .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Box A distribution of the per-cell weight E[w]/uniform, same construction as Box B.](osse_files/figure-html/fig-whist-a-output-1.png){#fig-whist-a width=1417 height=318} ::: ::: ::: On the analysis mask the advective array departs from uniform but not wildly: the per-cell weight has standard deviation $\approx 0.46$ (Box B) and $0.37$ (Box A) around a mean of $1$, most cells within a factor of two and the 99th percentile near $2\times$. Box B is the more preferential of the two, and its over-sampled cells cluster where the North Atlantic Current concentrates floats. The strongest concentration happens in shallow, sub-$2000$ m cells *outside* the mask, where it cannot enter $B$; what remains on-mask is the moderate structure shown here, consistent with the small measured bias. ## Bias as a covariance Take the $L^2(\mathbb{P})$ inner product $\langle f, g\rangle_{\mathbb{P}} = \int_{\mathcal{X}} f g\, \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}$, and let $q = w/p$ be the sampling frequency of each cell-day relative to its uniform share — the over/under-sampling factor mapped in @fig-wspace and distributed in @fig-whist, equal to $1$ under uniform sampling and with $\int q\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P} = 1$. The bias is the inner product of the field with the sampling excess, $$B_k \;=\; \langle \tilde Z_k,\, q - 1\rangle_{\mathbb{P}} \;=\; \langle \tilde Z_k - \bar Z_k,\, q - 1\rangle_{\mathbb{P}},$$ the second equality because $\langle 1, q-1\rangle_{\mathbb{P}} = 0$ — a spatially uniform field is sampled without bias. Cauchy–Schwarz for this inner product gives the cap $$|B_k| \;\le\; \lVert \tilde Z_k - \bar Z_k\rVert_{\mathbb{P}}\,\lVert q - 1\rVert_{\mathbb{P}} \;=\; \sigma_k \, \operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q),$$ with $\sigma_k = \operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(\tilde Z_k)$ (the residual-field table) and $\operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q)$ the spread of the over/under-sampling factor (@fig-whist), attained only when $q-1$ is proportional to the field anomaly. **Zero bias does not require uniform sampling** — it requires only that $q - 1$ be orthogonal to $\tilde Z_k$ in $L^2(\mathbb{P})$; a strongly non-uniform array ($\operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q) \gg 0$) can still be unbiased for this functional. $B_k$ is a *joint* spacetime inner product, so it does not reduce to the marginals mapped above, and the joint $\operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q)$ over the full cell-day grid is not cleanly estimable at a fixed realization count (a finite array occupies each cell-day at most a few times). We therefore report $B_k$'s exact split into a spatial-marginal covariance (the weight map against the time-mean field), a temporal-marginal covariance (the seasonal weight against the daily domain mean), and the space–time interaction that remains. ::: {#a68413a0 .cell execution_count=16} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}

The spatial-marginal component is real but modest, and the **space–time interaction is often the largest term** (Box B 2018 is almost entirely interaction): the array's spatial preference co-varies with the field's day-to-day structure, so the bias is a genuinely spatiotemporal covariance that the time-averaged weight map understates. On the scored years the spatial weight dispersion is $\operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q) \approx 0.46$ (Box B) and $0.37$ (Box A) against $\sigma_k$ of $6.3$–$7.6$ and $1.7$–$2.4$ GJ/m$^2$, so the Cauchy–Schwarz scale is a few GJ/m$^2$ and the realized $|B_k|$ is $\sim\!1$–$5\%$ of it: the sampling non-uniformity is largely, though not perfectly, orthogonal to the field. # Results ## Pilot specification The pilot is **$100$ independent realizations**. Each seeds **$1{,}000$ floats** uniformly over normalized space–time on the deep ($\mathrm{deptho}\ge 1000$ m) region spanning both boxes plus an $8^\circ$ margin, across $2010\text{-}01\text{-}01$ to $2019\text{-}12\text{-}26$, and advects them once at $1000$ m park depth ($10$-day profiling cycle, lifespans drawn from the real Argo record). Years $2010$–$2014$ are the equilibration lead; bias is scored on **$2015$–$2019$**. A profile enters an estimate when it falls inside a box, so the one deployment feeds both. Across all $100$ realizations the pilot seeds $10^5$ float-deployments and scores about $2.15$ million in-box profiles (the table below). Per realization, Box B holds $\sim\!90$ distinct floats (standing stock $\sim\!40$) giving $\sim\!1{,}410$–$1{,}490$ profiles a year; Box A holds $\sim\!145$ floats (stock $\sim\!78$) giving $\sim\!2{,}730$–$2{,}900$ — its quiescent flow retains more of the same deployment. ::: {#1da4399e .cell execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ```{=html}

It warrants scrutiny (real park depths and coverage differ from the simulation) but is a concrete, testable difference. ## Within-design dependence A design's $n$ profiles are not $n$ independent draws: each float profiles every $10$ days and lingers, so its consecutive cycles are near-replicates of one location. The float-clustered **design effect** is the resulting variance inflation, $$\mathrm{deff}_k \;=\; \frac{\sum_f \big(\sum_{i \in f}(\tilde Z_i - \hat Z)\big)^2} {\sum_i (\tilde Z_i - \hat Z)^2}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{n}{\mathrm{deff}_k},$$ summing over floats $f$: if a float's cycles were identical it contributes its cluster size to $\mathrm{deff}$, if independent it contributes $\approx 1$. The effective sample size is $n/\mathrm{deff}$, and the per-deployment spread inflates by $\approx\!\sqrt{\mathrm{deff}}$ over an iid design of the same $n$. ::: {#2031341b .cell execution_count=27} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ```{=html}

One caveat: the bootstrap's in-box standing stock ($\sim\!15$) is below real Argo's ($\sim\!27$–$30$) because the real array also draws floats deployed outside the seed region that drift in; in-box profile counts still match ($\sim\!500$/yr), so the $n$-independent mean-bias comparison holds. # Conclusions From this $100$-realization pilot: **The advective sampling bias is small but not zero.** In both boxes $\mathbb{E}[B_k]$ stays within $\sim\!0.02\,\sigma_k$ (the bias tables) — a few hundredths of a GJ/m$^2$ against a field varying by $6$–$8$ (Box B) and $2$ (Box A) GJ/m$^2$. It is not identically zero: several years are resolved at $2$–$4$ Monte-Carlo standard errors, so the array is weakly preferential in effect, at a magnitude that is a small fraction of the field's own variability. **Strong non-uniform sampling, nearly orthogonal to the field.** The array samples space genuinely non-uniformly (on-mask up to $\sim\!3.6\times$ over-sampling, $\operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q)\approx0.4$; @fig-whist), yet the bias is only $\sim\!1$–$5\%$ of the Cauchy–Schwarz ceiling that non-uniformity permits, i.e. a weight–field correlation $|\rho_k|\approx0.02$. Preferential sampling does not imply preferential bias for this functional — the estimand-level bias is the covariance $\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb{P}}(q,\tilde Z_k)$, and the array sits near its null space, not a property of sampling non-uniformity per se. **The bias is irreducibly spatiotemporal.** The temporal marginal is zero by construction and the spatial marginal is modest; the space–time interaction dominates (the decomposition table). The bias comes from the array's spatial preference co-varying with the field's day-to-day structure, so a time-averaged sampling map understates it and any correction must be posed jointly in space–time. **It is invisible in a single deployment.** The scatter of one array ($\operatorname{sd}(B)\approx0.3$ Box B, $0.09$ Box A; @fig-bias-intervals) is $5$–$10\times$ the mean bias. The systematic effect exists only in expectation over many arrays; a single year's estimate from one array is realization noise, not bias. **Profile counts overstate information.** Within-float clustering gives design effects of $\approx3$ (Box B) and $\approx5$ (Box A), so $n_{\mathrm{eff}}\sim550$ in both despite Box A's $\sim\!2\times$ larger $n$ (the design-effect table). **Both regimes are comparably biased once standardized.** Box B has larger raw bias and spread, but on the $\sigma_k$ scale the energetic western-boundary region is not disproportionately biased relative to the quiescent gyre. **The design and pipeline work.** Uniform space–time seeding plus a multi-year lead produces a stable equilibrium array with no calibrated schedule (the standing-stock table), and the $n$-matched uniform reference recovers $\mathbb{E}[B]=0$, so any advective departure is signal. ## Caveats - **Pilot precision.** $100$ realizations give a Monte-Carlo se of $\sim\!0.03$ (Box B) / $\sim\!0.01$ (Box A) GJ/m$^2$; the "small bias" conclusion is robust, but per-year signs and magnitudes are not all resolved and would sharpen with more realizations. - **The temporal null is assumed, not found** — the fixed $10$-day cadence, uniform release phase, and equilibrium stock remove any seasonal sampling preference by construction, so this is not evidence that a real array (with deployment surges, under-ice gaps, or seasonal mortality) carries none. - **Five scored years.** Deployment from $2010$ scores $2015$–$2019$; the velocity record now reaches $2005$, so extending to $2010$–$2019$ would double the field years at no new modelling cost. - **Array density.** The virtual array holds $\sim\!40$ (Box B) / $\sim\!78$ (Box A) floats against real Argo's $\sim\!27$ / $\sim\!30$ (the standing-stock table); $\mathbb{E}[B_k]$ is $n$-independent so it stands, but single-array spreads are density-specific. - **The mean field is a preliminary stationary trend-plus-harmonics fit** (@sec-meanfield); it sets the estimand's level but $B$ is invariant to it, so the conclusions above do not depend on it. - **No tight distribution-free bound yet.** We report the realized covariance and its decomposition; a bound over an RKHS smoothness class for $\tilde Z_k$ is the natural next step to turn "small in this pilot" into "provably bounded."
